                                          PROJECT NO. 58481

    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                           § PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §
    STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                     §            OF TEXAS


               COMMENTS OF MONARCH ENERGY DEVELOPMENT LLC
                      ON PROPOSED NEW 16 TAC §25.194

         COMES NOW Monarch Energy Development LLC (Monarch) and files these comments

regarding the Commission’s proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §25.194, relating

to Large Load Interconnection Standards. The proposed rule would set forth the standards and

criteria for an electric utility to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission

network. The Commission has requested that comments be filed by April 17, 2026, and therefore

these comments are timely filed.

     INTRODUCTION AND REQUEST FOR COMMISSION GUIDANCE TO ERCOT

         Monarch has already filed two sets of comments on proposed new 16 TAC §25.194. In the

first set of comments filed on March 4, 2026 1 in response to the Commission Staff’s draft Proposal

for Publication, Monarch addressed three issues:

         1. Large Load Projects that have already signed interconnection agreements and posted
            financial security should not be subject to retroactive requirements through ERCOT’s
            Batch Zero Process as proposed in Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145 that
            would essentially reject all progress and investments that have been made on the
            projects. Imposing new eligibility requirements on projects that have already satisfied
            prior ERCOT processes and committed substantial capital constitutes retroactive
            rulemaking that undermines regulatory certainty and investment-backed expectations.
         2. Large Load Projects should have more options regarding how to demonstrate site
            control at the Intermediate Agreement phase.
         3. The $100,000/MW financial security requirement for the intermediate agreement
            should be fully refundable after the payment of actual costs prudently incurred.




1
     Interchange Item 113, Monarch Energy Comments on Proposal for Publication.
         Monarch appreciates that the Commission acted on two of these issues (site control and the

magnitude of financial security) before it voted to publish the proposed new rule at its Open

Meeting on March 12, 2026.

        On March 19, 2026, Monarch filed additional comments in this proceeding. 2 In those

comments, Monarch again urged the Commission to increase the refundability of the financial

security (or an interconnection fee) in the amount of $50,000/MW that ERCOT proposes in PGRR

145 to require large load customers to post in order to even be eligible to be studied in the Large

Load Batch Study process. In addition, Monarch again urged the Commission to prohibit ERCOT

from imposing retroactive requirements through PGRR 145 that would essentially reject all

progress and investments that have been made over years of work on these projects and require

these large load customers to demonstrate again that they are “real” and be subject to limited, if

any, allocation for capacity to connect to the grid. These large loads have (i) signed interconnection

agreements with their transmission service provider (TSP), (ii) completed all requirements under

Planning Guide Sections 9.4 and 9.5, including having ERCOT-approved studies, and (iii)

demonstrated material financial commitment through Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC),

posting of financial security, and procurement of long-lead equipment. These large load customers

have already demonstrated that they meet an objective and administrable standard for non-

speculative load. As a result, the Commission should recognize these criteria as the appropriate

standard for identifying committed large load projects and provide guidance to ERCOT to ensure

that such projects are treated as Base Load that is not subject to additional study or re-screening as

proposed in PGRR 145.




2
    Interchange Item 125, Monarch Energy Comments on Proposal for Publication.

                                                                      Monarch Energy Comments - Page 2
         In its April 4, 2026, comments on PGRR 145, ERCOT has urged stakeholders to file

comments on these and other issues in order for the Commission to provide guidance to ERCOT

on how ERCOT should address these issues in the development of the Large Load Batch Study

process as documented in PGRR 145. 3 Accordingly, Monarch Energy respectfully requests that

the Commission provide clarifications to the issues that Monarch has raised above.



           COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC SECTIONS OF THE PROPOSED RULE

(d) Intermediate Agreement.

        Paragraph (d)(1) of the proposed rule provides several options for demonstrating site

control of property prior to an interconnection study being conducted. As noted above, Monarch

supports the inclusion of proposed paragraph (C), which allows for site control to be demonstrated

with an agreement with an option to purchase or lease land to accommodate the project at the

proposed location. This approach is generally used for large industrial developments, including for

the development of new generation resources.

        Monarch also appreciates that the Commission modified the proposed rule prior to

publication to have paragraph (10) require financial security in the amount of $50,000 per MW of

requested peak demand instead of $100,000 per MW. As discussed below regarding subsections

(g) and (h), though, Monarch continues to oppose the proposal that only 20% of this financial

security is refundable after paying all costs incurred.




3
    See, e.g., PGRR 145, Batch Zero Process for Large Load Interconnections, ERCOT Comments 040426, at 5-6
    (response to Satoshi Energy); 9-10 (response to Crow Holdings); 10 (response to Monarch Energy); 13-14
    (response to Satoshi Energy); 14-15 (response to Schaper); 15-16 (response to Crusoe); 20 (response to Schaper);
    26-27 (response to Skybox Datacenters); 30 (response to Crusoe); 32-33 (response to Crusoe); and 33-34
    (response to Skybox Datacenters).

                                                                           Monarch Energy Comments - Page 3
 (f) Interconnection Agreement.

       Paragraph (f)(1) of the proposed rule provides several options for demonstrating site

control of property when the large load customer executes the interconnection agreement. As noted

above, Monarch supports the inclusion of proposed paragraph (C), which allows for site control to

be demonstrated with a signed and executed purchase and sales agreement. This approach is

generally used for large industrial developments, including for the development of new generation

resources.

       Monarch Energy opposes the inclusion of paragraph (f)(10), which would require large

load customers to fund system upgrades that are remote from their point of direct interconnection

to the grid. This proposal is potentially the most disruptive to existing ERCOT transmission policy

and would be a major departure from past policy. The postage stamp transmission policy is one of

the most fundamental building blocks that has been in place since ERCOT’s transition to

competition, and has been a fundamental reason why generation and large load resources have

been better able to locate in the ERCOT region than other parts of the United States and customers

have been able to locate in the state without concern that they may shoulder much higher

transmission costs than other parts of the state. Unwinding the current postage stamp transmission

policy opens a whole Pandora’s Box. This process would create uncertainty and complexity by

inserting the concept of preferential access to the transmission system, in contravention of this

state’s long-standing policy for open and nondiscriminatory access to transmission. The core

principle of open and nondiscriminatory access that undergirds the existing competitive ERCOT

market should be considered sacrosanct, and therefore we oppose this policy change.

       For these reasons, Monarch Energy recommends that (f)(10) be deleted in its entirety as

follows:



                                                                Monarch Energy Comments - Page 4
        (10)    Financial security for system upgrades. A large load customer must post
               financial security for system upgrades that are necessary to reliably serve the large
               load customer not later than the date that the interconnection agreement is executed.
               (A)     The interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP may accept the
                       following forms of financial security for system upgrades:
                       (i)      cash collateral;
                       (ii)     corporate or parental guaranty, only if the corporation or parent
                                corporation has a credit rating equivalent of BBB-/Baa3 or higher
                                from Standard & Poor’s or Moody’s; or
                       (iii) a letter of credit issued by a major U.S. commercial bank, or a U.S.
                                branch office of a major foreign commercial bank, with a credit
                                rating of at least “A-” by Standard & Poor’s or “A3” by Moody’s
                                Investor Service.
               (B)     If the large load customer provides a corporate or parental guaranty under
                       this subsection, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP may
                       require the submission of financial records or statements to determine the
                       customer’s financial stability.
               (C)     Refund of financial security posted for system upgrades is subject to
                       subsections (g) through (i) of this section.

(g) Withdrawal of all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak demand.

       Pursuant to proposed paragraphs (g)(3) and (g)(4), the proposed rule would allow the

interconnecting TSP to retain up to 80% of the balance of financial security posted by the large

load during the intermediate phase if the load reduces or withdraws its proposed project. Monarch

understands that the premise for requiring the posting of this amount of financial security is

intended to ensure that proposed projects are “real.” As proposed, and as discussed above, the

financial security requirement acts as a penalty to deter the development of “real” projects since

the mostly non-refundable nature of this financial security is arbitrary and not connected to actual

costs incurred. This financial security should be fully refundable after payment for actual costs

that are prudently incurred in this phase of the process. If this financial security is not refundable,

then Monarch would recommend that the proposed rule be revised to incorporate a phased

approach to the posting of financial security that Chairman Gleeson suggested in the March 12,



                                                                   Monarch Energy Comments - Page 5
 2026, Open Meeting that would tie the posting and refundability of financial security to reasonable

commercial development milestones.

       Monarch recommends modifying paragraphs (g)(3) and (4) as follows, with subsequent

paragraphs renumbered appropriately.

       (3)       After applying the large load customer’s financial security to any outstanding
                 amounts owed, the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP must refund
                 20% of the remaining balance to the large load customer within 60 days.
       (4)       After applying the financial security to any outstanding amounts owed and
                 refunding 20% of the balance, the remaining 80% of the balance must be paid to
                 the interconnecting TSP and applied by that TSP as an offset to the interconnecting
                 TSP’s rate base in the earlier of the interconnecting TSP’s next interim rate
                 proceeding or comprehensive rate proceeding.

(h) Non-utilized capacity.

       Subsection (h) establishes a process whereby an interconnecting TSP or DSP must notify

ERCOT if a large load customer fails to satisfy, by 6 months, a milestone in its schedule for phased

energization. The subsection further requires a draw down on financial security, partial refund, and

reallocation of non-utilized capacity. Monarch recommends that any process whereby a large load

customer may be subject to having awarded interconnection capacity revoked by the

interconnecting DSP, interconnecting TSP, or ERCOT should be based on a failure to use the

allocated load for more than a year, at a minimum, and also must be subject to the large load

customer having an opportunity to demonstrate good cause for the delayed utilization of that

capacity. There are many factors that can delay achieving a planned ramp schedule, especially

supply chain problems, failure of long lead time replacement equipment, or other unforeseen

circumstances.

       Similarly to subsection (g) discussed above, subsection (h)(3) and (4) would allow only 20

percent of any remaining financial security to be refunded to the large load customer, with the

remaining 80 percent being applied as an offset to ratebase. Again, this structure is unreasonable

                                                                 Monarch Energy Comments - Page 6
 and should be modified so that the non-refundable penalty to the customer is no more than 20

percent rather than 80 percent. For consistency, subsection (h) should be modified similarly to

mirror subsection (g).

       Finally, subsection (h)(5) states that CIAC is not refundable. However, if ERCOT

reallocates that customer’s capacity to a subsequent large load customer, and equipment or services

that the original customer paid for through CIAC are used to support the interconnection of the

subsequent customer, then subsequent customer should be charged CIAC to pay for the upgrades

that they are now using for themselves, and the original customer should receive a refund from the

electric utility for the cost of that equipment or services. At a minimum, the language should be

modified to allow for a refund to a large load customer within 60 days if the capacity is reassigned

to another customer. Additionally, we recommend that the Commission clarify that CIAC is

refundable to the extent the amount paid exceeds the actual costs incurred. Paragraph (f)(9)(C)

allows for refund of financial security posted for system upgrades, and given that refunds are

allowed under those circumstances, it is appropriate to allow for refunds for withdrawal of all or a

portion of requested or contracted peak demand for interconnection.

                                         CONCLUSION

       Monarch appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and respectfully requests

that the Commission adopt a rule with modifications consistent with these comments.

 Dated: April 15, 2026
                                                                          Respectfully submitted,


                                                              ______________/s/_____________
                                                                              Kevin Boudreaux
                                                                         Head of Power Supply
                                                              Monarch Energy Development LLC
                                                                                (832) 875-0969
                                                                  KBoudreaux@monarch.energy

              included in Batch Zero as “Base Load not Subject to Additional Study in the Batch
              Zero Process” as proposed in PGRR 145.
 •   (d), Intermediate agreement:
          o Monarch supports (d)(1)(C), which allows for site control to be demonstrated with
              an agreement with an option to purchase or lease land.
          o Monarch appreciates that the Commission modified the proposed rule prior to
              publication to have paragraph (10) require financial security in the amount of
              $50,000 per MW of requested peak demand instead of $100,000 per MW. However,
              Monarch continues to oppose the proposal that only 20% of this financial security
              is refundable after paying all costs incurred.
 •   (f), Interconnection agreement:
          o Monarch supports the inclusion of (f)(1)(C), which allows for site control to be

 •   (g), Withdrawal of all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak demand:
          o Financial security should be fully refundable after payment for actual costs that are
              prudently incurred in this phase of the process. If this financial security is not
              refundable, then Monarch would recommend that the proposed rule be revised to

                                                                Monarch Energy Comments - Page 8
            incorporate a phased approach to the posting of financial security that Chairman
           Gleeson suggested in the March 12, 2026, Open Meeting that would tie the posting
           and refundability of financial security to reasonable commercial development
           milestones.
•   (h), Non-utilized capacity:
        o The non-refundable penalty should be modified to be no more than 20 percent
           rather than 80 percent.
        o Regarding CIAC in (h)(5), if ERCOT reallocates that customer’s capacity to a
           subsequent large load customer, and equipment or services that the original
           customer paid for through CIAC are used to support the interconnection of the
           subsequent customer, then the subsequent customer should be charged CIAC to pay

           Additionally, we recommend that the Commission clarify that CIAC is refundable

           allows for refund of financial security posted for system upgrades, and given that
           refunds are allowed under those circumstances, it is appropriate to allow for refunds

           interconnection.
